messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mateo has always seen the world in terms of order and consequence, a perspective honed by forty years as a prosecutor. At sixty-seven, a widower with a formidable courtroom presence, he presented as a man in absolute control. Yet, for the past eight months, his meticulously structured life has been collapsing inward, ever since a family gathering at his brother’s home. The assault happened in the basement, perpetrated by a younger relative he had trusted. While his grandchildren’s laughter echoed from the yard outside, the cold, damp concrete floor pressed against his skin, a detail now seared into his mind with terrifying clarity. This memory, he explained, is not a memory at all; it is a recurring event.

The triggers are insidious and everywhere. A cool draft from an office air conditioning vent brushing against his arm is enough to plunge him back into the basement. In these moments, the memory isn't recalled; it erupts. The stale, musty smell fills his nostrils, the rough texture of the concrete is on his back, and the feeling of powerlessness is absolute, as if it is happening for the first time, right now. This visceral re-experiencing immediately activates a primal sense of threat. His gaze, once focused and analytical, now darts around the courtroom, not to read the jury, but to locate the exits, his mind cataloging the bailiff's sidearm or the sharp edge of the witness stand lectern as potential weapons. The memory forces him to see danger everywhere, because in that moment, the danger feels present and real.

This intrusive memory brings with it a cascade of devastating self-appraisals. Each time the scene plays out in his mind, it reinforces a sickening belief that he is permanently contaminated. He described a feeling of being "unclean" that no amount of showering can wash away, a deep sense of physical violation that has left his body irrevocably damaged and weak. This belief that he is now fundamentally broken serves as its own kind of trigger, constantly pulling his thoughts back to the basement as if searching for the exact moment he was ruined. This conviction of his own defilement and fragility has fundamentally altered his perception of the world. He had come to believe that the world is not a place of laws and reason, but a landscape of hidden, unpredictable violence. This belief system is what fuels his constant threat-monitoring; if he is broken and the world is dangerous, then vigilance is the only logical response. He finds himself unable to enter a new restaurant or shop without first assessing its layout for escape routes, a habit that has made him avoid any unfamiliar place altogether.

His internal state of high alert only serves to prime him for more intrusions. The simple act of scanning a room for threats makes him hyper-aware of his surroundings, which in turn makes him more likely to encounter a trigger. The cool leather of his office chair or the low hum of the building’s ventilation can now hijack his attention, and because his system is already primed for danger, these neutral sensations are interpreted as imminent threats, which in turn yanks the memory back to the forefront of his mind. In this way, his attempts to stay safe only make the world feel more threatening and the memories more accessible.

The negative beliefs he holds about himself are now the lens through which he views his entire life, colouring his relationships and experiences. The deeply held conviction that he is contaminated makes any reminder of family, especially children, almost unbearable. An invitation to his grandson’s birthday party is no longer a source of joy but a trigger for intense shame. The thought of being around his grandchildren, the very sound of their voices, now brings an immediate and overwhelming sense of his own unworthiness and filth. This cycle has become self-perpetuating; the belief that he is dirty makes him fear his family, and any contact with them confirms and deepens that terrible belief. His life, once rich with family and professional pride, has shrunk to the path between his empty house and his office. He finally sought therapy after he was unable to attend his granddaughter’s baptism, realizing that the isolation he had constructed to protect himself had become a prison. His primary hope, he stated with quiet desperation, is not just to forget, but to one day be able to hold his grandchildren again without feeling like he is poisoning them with his touch.
